heading: Fair Work system
text: Learn who’s covered by the Fair Work system and what that means for workplace rights and responsibilities. On this page: What is the Fair Work System Key features of the Fair Work system Who is covered by the Fair Work system Before the Fair Work Ombudsman Tools and resources Related information

heading: What is the Fair Work system
text: The Fair Work systemA national workplace relations system introduced by the Fair Work Act 2009 that provides for the minimum employment standards and regulates on a range of employment and industrial matters. (www.fairwork.gov.au/taxonomy/term/472) was created by the Fair Work Act 2009 and started on 1 July 2009. The Fair Work system is the name used for the minimum employment laws and agency bodies that were created by the Fair Work Act 2009. It's the na- tional workplace relations systemThe national work- place relations system is a collection of legislation that applies to most employees and employers in Australia. It includes the Fair Work Act 2009, the National Employment Standards, registered agree- ments and awards. (www.fairwork.gov.au/taxonomy/term/406) . For a brief outline of Australia's workplace relations law, visit the Australia's industrial relations timeline (www.fairwork.gov.au/about-us/workplace-laws/fair- work-system/australias-industrial-relations-timeline) page.

heading: system
text: The key features of the Fair Work system are: the minimum National Employment Standards (www.fairwork.gov.au/employment- conditions/national-employment-standards) awards (www.fairwork.gov.au/node/327) that apply nationally for specific industries and occupations the National Minimum WageA pay rate that applies to employees not covered by an award or regis- tered agreement. Certain award or agreement free employees may have different pay entitlements depending on whether they have a reduced work capacity because of disability, if they're under the age of 21 or if they are an apprentice or trainee. (www.fairwork.gov.au/taxonomy/term/404) protection from unfair dismissal (www.fairwork.gov.au/ending-employment/help- with-termination/unfair-dismissal) . The National Employment Standards, awards and the National Minimum Wage make up a safety net of entitlements for employeesA person that’s hired to perform work for a company either on a full-time, part- time or casual basis in exchange for payment. Other known terms: staff and worker. (www.fairwork.gov.au/taxonomy/term/516) covered by the Fair Work system. Other workplace participants in the Fair Work system (such as regulated workersA person who is an employee-like worker or a regulated road transport contractor. (www.fairwork.gov.au/taxonomy/term/795) ) have different rights and entitlements. There are several key bodies that have roles in the Fair Work system: Fair Work Ombudsman (us) Fair Work Commission (https://www.fwc.gov.au/) Fair Work Division of the Federal Court (https://www.fedcourt.gov.au/) and the Federal Circuit and Family Court (https://www.fcfcoa.gov.au/) .

heading: Work system
text: The Fair Work system (the national system) covers most Australian workplaces. Working out who is covered is important because we work with those covered by the national system. There are some Fair Work system entitlements that will apply to employers and employees who aren't in the national system. For more information read our Library article - Non-national system employee enti- tlements in the Fair Work Act 2009 (https://library.fairwork.gov.au/viewer/?krn=K600442) . Tip: Ask your state or territory body or workplace for help Employers and employees who aren’t covered by the Fair Work system should contact the relevant state body or their internal human resources department for help. Check who isn't covered in your state or territory by selecting from the list below: Australian Capital Territory and Northern Territory New South Wales South Australia Queensland Tasmania Victoria Western Australia

heading: Northern Territory
text:
Generally, all employees and employers in the Australian Capital Territory and Northern Territory are covered by the national system.

### New South Wales
State public sector and local government employees aren't covered by the national system and remain under the state system.

heading: South Australia
text:
State public sector and local government employees aren't covered by the national system and remain under the state system.

### Queensland
State public sector and local government employees aren't covered by the national system and remain under the state system.

heading: Tasmania
text:
State public sector employees remain under the state system. Local government employees are covered by the national system.

### Victoria
Most employees in Victoria are covered by the national system. This includes state government employees with some exceptions such as senior public servants.

heading: Western Australia
text: All Western Australian State public sector employers are covered by the state industrial relations system. The following types of businesses are also covered by the state system: sole traders partnerships other unincorporated entities non-trading corporations. If a business is run by a sole trader in Western Australia and changes to a company, it may move to the national system. If a business is run by a partnership in Western Australia, the partnership will usually qualify as a national system employer if one of the partners is: a company engaged in sufficient trading or financial activities.

heading: Local government employers
text: From 1 January 2023, all Western Australian local government entities are covered by the state system. This is because of a state declaration endorsed by the federal Minister. Before 1 January 2023, Western Australian local government entities may have been covered by the national or the state system. To learn more about who's covered by the state system in Western Australia, visit the Department of Local Government, Industry Regulation and Safety: Which system of employment laws applies (https://www.wa.gov.au/organisation/private-sector- labour-relations/which-system-of-employment-laws- applies) . For information about different business structures, visit Business Structures - Business.gov.au (https://business.gov.au/planning/business-structures- and-types/business-structures) .
